---
title: "Building Real-Time Pipelines"
format: html
---

Building a production-grade streaming pipeline is a complete departure from
batch engineering. System changes — a user click, an IoT temperature spike, a
financial transaction — are instantly broadcast as individual event objects,
typically structured as JSON, Avro, or Protobuf payloads, rather than waiting
to land in a daily export. Data is no longer a bounded file with a beginning
and an end — it's an **unbounded dataset**: a continuous, append-only series
of events that never finishes arriving. Producers and consumers stay **loosely
coupled**, talking only through the broker, never directly to each other. To
design for that, engineers need to understand what actually happens inside
the broker and the processor sitting on top of it.

## A minimal streaming pipeline in Python

Before reaching for Kafka itself, it's worth seeing the same producer /
broker / processor shape in miniature. This small simulator swaps Kafka for a
plain `asyncio.Queue` per topic channel:

```python
import asyncio
import json
import random
from datetime import datetime

# Simulating a High-Throughput Distributed Message Broker
class StreamBroker:
    def __init__(self):
        # Different message topic channels
        self.topics = {
            "iot_sensor_stream": asyncio.Queue(),
            "processed_alerts": asyncio.Queue(),
        }

    async def publish(self, topic, message):
        await self.topics[topic].put(message)

    async def consume(self, topic):
        return await self.topics[topic].get()
```

`temperature_sensor_producer` emits unstructured readings from two
independent sensors, `SENSOR_A` and `SENSOR_B`, onto `iot_sensor_stream`,
smoothly and without caring who — if anyone — is reading them.
`StreamBroker` itself handles the concurrent ingress of both streams safely;
it doesn't know or care that two producers are publishing at once, since each
call just drops a message onto the appropriate queue. On the other side,
`anomaly_detection_stream_processor` consumes from that same queue and parses
each incoming event in real time, running an instant mathematical threshold
check and publishing anything that trips it onto `processed_alerts` — all
without ever storing data in an intermediate relational table.

## Kafka: partitions, offsets, and consumer groups

A Kafka **topic** isn't a single log — it's split into **N ordered, immutable
partitions**, and every message is routed to exactly one of them. Within a
partition, each message gets a monotonically increasing **offset**, which is
simply its address: "message #4,213 in partition 2."

Consumers read as a **consumer group**: a set of workers that jointly consume
a topic, with every partition assigned to exactly one member of the group at a
time. That assignment is what sets the pipeline's real throughput ceiling —
**adding consumers beyond the partition count gives zero extra parallelism**,
because there's nothing left to hand them.

| Concept | What it is | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Partition | One ordered, immutable log within a topic | Unit of parallelism — more partitions, more concurrent consumers |
| Offset | A message's position within its partition | Lets a consumer say exactly where it is |
| Consumer group | A set of consumers sharing a topic's partitions | Each partition goes to one member only |
| Offset commit | A consumer checkpoints its current position | Crash recovery resumes from the last committed offset, not from zero |
| Rebalance | Partition reassignment when a member joins or leaves | Keeps the group's load balanced automatically |

## Window types: tumbling, sliding, session

A stream never "ends," so aggregations (sums, averages, counts) need a
boundary to close over. That boundary is a **window**, and the three common
shapes solve different problems:

| Window type | Shape | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| **Tumbling** | Fixed-size, non-overlapping — every event belongs to exactly one window | Hourly sales totals — clean, non-overlapping reporting periods |
| **Sliding** | Fixed-size, overlapping — one event can appear in multiple windows | Rolling 5-minute average CPU load — overlap is needed to catch a spike right at a window boundary |
| **Session** | Gap-based — the window closes after N seconds of inactivity; size varies per session | Click-stream grouping — a user's session ends after 30+ minutes idle |

The lab's `StreamProcessor` (in [Day2_Lab.ipynb](Day2_Lab.ipynb)) implements
both a **tumbling** window (one-second buckets, used for a per-second event
count) and a **sliding** window (a rolling 3-second average temperature) side
by side over the same event stream, so you can see both update independently
as events arrive.

## Watermarks: handling late-arriving data

Network delays mean an event timestamped `T` can physically arrive at the
processor at `T + 5 minutes`. A **watermark** is a declared threshold that
answers "how long am I willing to wait for a late event before I close the
window and move on?" — in Spark Structured Streaming:

```python
stream.withWatermark("event_time", "5 minutes")
```

Anything that arrives after the watermark has already passed is either
dropped or routed to a dead-letter side output. The trade-off is direct: a
larger watermark buys more completeness at the cost of higher latency; a
smaller one returns results faster but drops more late data. Set it from the
**observed p99 latency** of the actual data source — not the theoretical
worst case, which would make every window wait far longer than necessary.

## Exactly-once delivery — the hard problem

Every streaming system has to pick a delivery guarantee, and the honest
options trade off against each other:

| Guarantee | Behavior | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| At-most-once | Fire and forget | Fastest, but silent data loss on failure — never acceptable for financial or audit data |
| At-least-once | Retry on failure | No data loss, but duplicates are possible — the most common default |
| Exactly-once | No loss, no duplicates | Requires coordination between producer, broker, *and* consumer |

Kafka reaches exactly-once with `enable.idempotence=true`, the transactional
producer API, and `isolation.level=read_committed` on the consumer side. Flink
reaches it with two-phase-commit checkpointing, which only works if the sink
itself supports transactions (Kafka, JDBC, Iceberg all do). Either way,
exactly-once isn't free — it adds roughly **20% throughput overhead** — so pay
for it only where a duplicate would cause real harm (a double-charged payment,
a double-counted fraud alert), not for every topic in the system by default.

## Ingestion, transformation, orchestration

Every pipeline — batch or streaming — still breaks down into the same three
stages; only the tools and latency budget change.

| Stage | Purpose | Typical tools |
|---|---|---|
| **Ingestion** | Pull raw data from external systems into central storage | Apache Kafka, Debezium, Fivetran, AWS Kinesis |
| **Transformation** | Clean, filter, and structure the raw data | Apache Spark, dbt, PySpark, Pandas |
| **Orchestration** | Schedule tasks, manage dependencies, handle errors across the whole system | Apache Airflow, Prefect, Dagster |

Ingestion is the vacuum cleaner gathering raw material — user clicks,
database updates, application logs — from wherever it's generated into
central storage. Transformation is the factory turning that raw material into
a usable product: filtering out noise, deduplicating records, and converting
messy raw files into the standard tables downstream AI models and analytical
tools can actually read. Orchestration is the conductor making sure every
stage runs in the right order and recovers cleanly when something fails.

## Lab: a real-time streaming pipeline with Kafka and Delta Lake

The [Day 2 lab notebook](Day2_Lab.ipynb) puts every concept above into one
runnable pipeline, in two parts. It leans on `asyncio` for the concurrent
streaming loops, pins `pyspark==3.5.0` alongside `delta-spark==3.5.0` to
manage the Lakehouse storage sink, and otherwise sticks to the standard
library for the math.

**Part 1 — mock Kafka streaming pipeline.** A `MockKafkaBroker` (built on
`asyncio.Queue`, with partitions and offsets modeled explicitly) receives
readings from three concurrent factory-sensor producers
(`CNC_MILL_01`, `ROBOTIC_ARM_02`, `ASSEMBLY_LINE_03`), each flooding the
broker independently without talking to each other or locking on any shared
thread state. A `StreamProcessor` consumes them and applies all three
concepts from this page at once: a tumbling window (per-second event counts),
a sliding window (a 3-second rolling average that keeps readings in memory
only for that active span and evicts anything older to keep memory bounded),
and a watermark (dropping anything older than 2 seconds). Anything over
threshold gets published to an `anomalies_sink` topic, which a Delta Lake
writer appends transactionally, turning the transient micro-batches back into
durable, queryable structured logs — the same ACID guarantees from Day 1, now
on a live stream instead of a static file.

**Part 2 — a real Kafka round trip.** The mock broker never touches the
actual `kafka-python` client, and a real capstone pipeline needs schema
validation at the edge. This part runs one real `KafkaProducer` →
topic → `KafkaConsumer` round trip, gated by a Pydantic model
(`SensorReading`) that rejects a deliberately malformed message (a
`temperature` sent as the string `"not_a_number"`) instead of letting it crash
the consumer.

::: {.callout-note}
Running Part 1's Delta sink locally on Windows requires a `winutils.exe` /
`HADOOP_HOME` setup for PySpark — a standard PySpark-on-Windows limitation,
not a bug in the notebook (see the same caveat on
[Day 1](../L01/01_lakehouse_architectures.qmd)). It runs cleanly on Colab
(Linux) or macOS/Linux with no extra setup. The notebook's own saved output
for Part 1 was captured from a real executed run on Colab.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Part 2 needs a real, running Kafka broker on `localhost:9092` — the notebook
includes the commands to start a local single-broker Kafka directly in Colab
(KRaft mode, no Zookeeper needed). The output saved in this notebook was
captured from a real run in an environment with `kafka-python` and `pydantic`
installed but **no broker listening** — which is exactly what you'll see if
you run this cell without first starting Kafka: the schema-gate code catches
the failure and prints clear setup instructions instead of a raw stack trace,
rather than crashing. To see the full accept/reject round trip (two valid
readings accepted, one malformed reading rejected by `SensorReading`'s
validator), start the broker first, per the notebook's own instructions.
:::
